To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The proposed architecture of the query processing and rule management system is suitable for use on a local area network with multiple workstations.

(i) the use of multiple computers in the same network as a data server to derive rules from database subsets can significantly speed up rule derivation; and (ii) the use of such computers to maintain the derived rules is also effective, but less so.

a) it is possible to use a set of work-stations in a LAN to derive and maintain a large set of rules describing subsets of a database table, b) the performance of the query processing system is not significantly affected by the presence of these workstations, and c) the performance of query processing can be improved by using the derived rules.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of spare computing capacity in a local area network to derive and maintain a set of rules describing data in subsets in a relational database.
the development of a prototype data server which can be used in a network of workstations for query optimisation using rules derived from subsets of a database.
the use of a networked computer as a database server to provide a query interface to one or many database management systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of a multiple workstation environment is feasible, and that there is a significant improvement in performance over the single workstation environment.
the use of multiple computers to derive rules is a viable option.
the use of multiple networked computers to derive and maintain a set of rules for query optimisation can be an efficient way of reducing the workload on the database server.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of multiple computers in the network for rule derivation and maintenance is feasible and can be effective in speeding up query processing.

it is possible to utilise the spare computing power of a network of computers to derive and maintain a set of rules describing subsets in a database and use these rules for semantically optimising queries.

it is feasible to utilise spare computing capacity in a local area network to derive rules from database subsets, and that this can be done in a way that does not interfere with the data server's query processing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the problem of rule derivation and maintenance is a good candidate for parallelisation and distributed computation.

it is possible to utilise spare capacity on multiple computers in a local area network to perform the work of rule derivation and rule maintenance without affecting the performance of the data server.
a single computer in a local area network can use a number of other computers to derive and maintain subset-descriptor rules to use in query reformulation.
